title: Pricing by hours per project for Garden maintenance and clean-ups
audience: Owners and supervisors of garden maintenance and clean-up crews who write quotes and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate clean-up hours, including loading, travel to the disposal point and checking time
Build a garden quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A clean-up is mostly labour, and its hours change with the state of the garden. A neglected bed with weeds, bark and cuttings takes far longer than the same bed kept up. Hours make that difference visible. A flat price with no hours behind it hides the risk and the waste, and it cannot be defended when a client asks why a clean-up costs what it does.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Divide the year's total cost of running the crew by its chargeable hours. Include wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation (business.gov.au, updated 1 October 2026), the vehicle and trailer, hand tools and power tools and their upkeep, fuel, disposal costs, insurance, administration and premises. Use chargeable hours, not paid hours. If you pay for 40 hours and 30 are spent on client gardens, the cost per productive hour is higher than the wage. Check the award or agreement that applies to each worker before using any wage figure, because this lesson does not state pay rates.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each clean-up into tasks: clearing beds, pulling weeds, cutting back, raking and blowing paths, loading, travel to the disposal point and checking. Estimate each task as a range from your own log, and add set-up, pack-down and travel as named lines. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as access problems and weather. Xero suggests a 10 to 20 per cent allowance for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026); size yours from your records. Compare quoted and actual labour after each job (Carters Trade Leader, 1 October 2025; New Zealand source, method only).

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour, add the margin for risk, such as a heavily overgrown bed or a steep site, and then price the green-waste line separately. Disposal is its own line, using the actual cost you pay. The Melbourne cost guide lists one trailer or ute load of green waste at $110 to $290 (What's the Damage, verified 1 November 2026). Use it as a market check, not as a disposal fee. The vendor ranges for a garden tidy-up ($120 to $300) and a green-waste add-on ($50 to $150) are also a check only (Airtasker, updated 18 June 2026).

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: The quote states the scope, the hours basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide (access, pot plants moved, pets kept inside), the green-waste line, GST status and validity. Do not show the internal cost per hour unless your policy says so. Re-quote when the scope changes, for example when a hidden stump or a much heavier load is found. Record the change in writing before the extra work starts (WA Consumer Protection, 4 September 2026).

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten clean-ups of each type. If the variance is consistently above your threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. Review prices about every three months (Business Victoria, undated).

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break the clean-up into tasks and estimate each task time as a range.
Add set-up, pack-down, loading, travel to the disposal point and checking time as named lines.
Multiply total crew hours by the cost per productive hour, add the delay allowance, then apply the margin.
Apply the materials and disposal policy and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs, GST status and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A clean-up of an 80 m² garden needs 4 crew-hours on site for clearing, cutting back and raking, plus 1 crew-hour for one trailer load to the disposal point and back. The owner's cost per productive hour is $55 (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative). The disposal fee is entered as a separate line at the owner's actual cost.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the labour cost, what is the labour price with a 25 per cent margin, and why does the disposal fee stay on its own line?
workedExamples.reasoning: The crew-hours total 5, so the labour cost is 5 multiplied by $55, which is $275. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is $275 divided by 0.75, which is $366.67 before the disposal fee. The disposal fee stays on its own line because it is a real cost that varies with the site and the disposal point, and the cost guide's load rate of $110 to $290 is a market check, not a disposal fee. The labour price is then compared with the vendor range of $170 to $450 for a tidy-up with a green-waste add-on. That range does not state how it treats GST, so the owner states the GST status on the quote.

equipmentAndPpe: Time log for each clean-up, with estimated and actual columns
Measuring tape or laser measure for bed and lawn areas

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle and trailer costs, tool upkeep, disposal, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out loading, travel and checking time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate.
List what is excluded, what the client provides, and the access assumptions.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each job and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). State and territory fair trading rules also apply and differ, so check the rules for your state.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. This lesson does not state those rates.
Green-waste disposal rules for a gardener are not confirmed in this lesson. Price the disposal from the actual cost and check council and EPA Victoria rules before writing the line.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs, GST status and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten clean-ups of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision, a disposal line and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions, disposal line, GST status and validity
Job time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make the work visible, so start every clean-up quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Loading, travel and checking time are named lines, and disposal is a separate line.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid worker and nothing else from the accounts or the rent
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and the crew bonus paid
The average hourly rate of competitors in the local area and their fees for the whole year
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, equipment, consumables, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A garden clean-up is estimated at 5 crew-hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a garden quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and to keep the rates a secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and to fill up the page with more text and words for the client
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and to make the job seem much smaller than it is

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly cost.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: divide by billable hours, not total hours; 10 to 20 per cent allowance for unexpected work.

Carters Trade Leader, 'Estimating how many hours a job will take: Why 83% get it wrong', https://tradeleader.carters.co.nz/trade-skills/estimating-how-many-hours-a-job-will-take-why-83-get-it-wrong/, dated 1 October 2025. New Zealand publisher; general method only. Supports: compare quoted and actual labour.

What's the Damage, 'Landscaping cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/landscaping-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026. Cost guide; not a regulator. Supports: green waste removal for one trailer or ute load $110 to $290.

Airtasker, 'How much does garden maintenance cost', https://www.airtasker.com/au/costs/garden-maintenance/how-much-does-garden-maintenance-cost, last updated 18 June 2026. Vendor marketplace; no stated method. Supports: garden tidy-up $120 to $300; green-waste add-on $50 to $150.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

WA Consumer Protection, 'Estimates, quotes and deposits', https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/estimates-quotes-and-deposits, last updated 4 September 2026. Western Australia only. Supports: record quote changes before extra work; total including GST.

EPA Victoria, 'A12: transporting waste out of Victoria', https://www.epa.vic.gov.au/a12-transporting-waste-out-victoria, 30 May 2025. Read for the green-waste gap: covers solid reportable priority waste only and does not mention garden waste.
